chapter_theme: Idaikkadar's cowherds continue. Thandavaraya Konar, to a drum refrain, claims the work done: the goat of the inner faculty and the forest of ignorance cut with the sword of tapas, the five sense-goats driven into the space of yoga, both attachments cut, the nectar drunk at the palate, the six centres passed to the Lord above them. Narayana Konar then speaks to his cow, the bound soul, promising release, the flight of karma and the gods' service to one who bows with love at the Lord's feet and clings to the void past pointing; the section to many begins, praising the light in the eye and the sun beyond mind, speech and body.
structure_note: 1757 is the drum refrain (தாந் திமித்திமி) printed once and marked (தாந்) after each of 1758 to 1765, Thandavaraya Konar's first-person stanzas of attainment and one of command (1765). 1766 to 1779 are Narayana Konar's quatrains, each with the call பசுவே (cow), which in Siddhanta also names the bound soul. 1780 and 1781 open the couplets to many (பலரோடு கிளத்தல், kural venchendurai), each ending போற்றீரே, praise, which run on into chapter 93. The herding images (goats for the senses and the inner faculty, the forest as pasture, the cow as soul) carry the teaching.

1757.reading: The refrain of the dance: drum-syllables (thaan thimithimi) addressed to the herdsman, who is hailed as the herdsman of bliss, of grace and bliss.
1757.nuance: The unit is the refrain sung after each of 1758 to 1765 (marked (தாந்) there). கோனார், herdsman, is both Thandavaraya Konar and, through தாண்டவம், the dancing Lord; the drum-syllables put the cowherd's song in the rhythm of Siva's dance.

1758.reading: I have seen the thousand and eight circles and what stood within that circle; I have looked at the hundred and eight of the great wide world, and the doubt that clings to a dull mind is gone.
1758.nuance: The numbers carry the sense and are not explained. The thousand and eight circles are most often taken as the thousand-petalled lotus at the crown, and what stands within it as the Lord there; the hundred and eight of the world may be shrines, scriptures or a sacred count. On a plain reading the boast is that inner sight has settled what outward search left in doubt.

1759.reading: With the sword of tapas in its measured rhythm I cut down the goat called the inner faculty and the dense forest called ignorance, and I built a fort to live without dying.
1759.nuance: அந்தக்கரணம், the inner instrument (mind, intellect, will and ego), is made the goat, the cowherd's own beast and the usual animal of sacrifice; the sacrifice is turned inward. The fort for not dying (சாவாது இருந்திட) is the claim of the body made deathless, as tradition takes the Siddhars' kaya siddhi; it can also be read as the soul made safe. சந்தம் may be rhythm or beauty.

1760.reading: The five goats called body, mouth, eye, nose and ear, and the forest of their objects, taste, light, touch and sound, I drove without shooting an arrow, wore them down and set them dancing, within the one space, the space of yoga.
1760.nuance: The senses are the herd and their objects the pasture; the herdsman masters them by driving, not by killing (எய்யாமல், without shooting). வீறு at the head of the objects is odd where smell is wanted and may be corrupt. ஏக வெளி and யோக வெளி, the one space and the yoga space, name where the herd is penned: the inner sky of the Siddhars.

1761.reading: With both attachments cut I came to good nature and friendship; I took in the milk and saw the eye above; I put away petty pleasure and looked to the other pleasure; I joined the supreme of consciousness and reached the supreme of the self.
1761.nuance: பற்றிரண்டு, the two attachments, are traditionally 'I' and 'mine'. The milk (பாலை) and the eye above (மேலையாம் கண்) are coded: tradition takes them as the nectar from the crown and the inner eye of the brow; in plain terms they are the sweetness and sight that come after detachment. சிற்பரம் and தற்பரம் are paired names of the Supreme, as consciousness and as the self's own highest.

1762.reading: Closing the palate within, I drink the nectar; I think then on the station in the sky; holding the word that rules the heavens I do worship; I go to nothing but true knowledge.
1762.nuance: அண்ணாக்கை அடைத்து, closing at the palate, is the yogic seal in which the tongue is turned back to block the passage and the nectar from the crown is drunk, as tradition reads it (Tirumular's khechari). The verbs in -ணேன் are ambiguous: the last line must mean 'I will not approach anything but knowledge', and some take the first three as refusals too, 'I will not drink, think, worship'; the run of claims in 1758 to 1763 favours the affirmative.

1763.reading: I have seen the five elements from earth up; I have broken from all the changes of maya; I have taken into my body the word of the ruler of the sky; I do not want life on earth as the higher thing.
1763.nuance: விண்டேனே may be 'I split off from' or 'I laid bare'; on either sense maya's transformations no longer hold the speaker. The word of the sky's ruler taken into the body (மெய்யினுள்) is the mantra or teaching made inward; மெய் also means truth, so it is held 'in truth' as well.

1764.reading: I have known well the five that begin with speech; I have parted from the five bonds of maya; I have practised the five yogas that are hard to see; I have cherished the vision of the fivefold yoga that is beyond telling.
1764.nuance: வாக்காதி ஐந்து are the five organs of action (speech, hands, feet, excretion, generation) among the tattvas. The five bonds of maya and the five yogas are not named; the fivefolds may answer the Lord's five acts or the five kalas, as tradition sometimes counts them. The stanza is a ledger of fives, more claim than teaching.

1765.reading: Seek the gods of the six supports; search for the Primal One above them; join the bliss of the circle that is his portion; see all five sheaths and climb the hill and dance.
1765.nuance: ஆறாதாரம் are the six centres of the yogic body, each with its presiding god; the Lord is placed above all six. கோசம் ஐந்து is most naturally the five sheaths of the self; an editor glosses கோசம் as the womb instead. The hill (குன்று) is the crown, as tradition takes it, and the dance answers the refrain's drum.

1766.reading: If you think with love on the Primal Lord, cow, will the supreme way of light not become your own?
1766.nuance: Narayana Konar's songs (1766 to 1779) each address பசுவே, 'cow'. In Saiva Siddhanta பசு is also the bound soul, so the herdsman talking to his cow is the teacher talking to the soul; the pun runs through the section. ஆதிபகவன் is the Kural's opening name for God.

1767.reading: If you think on the thing that fills everywhere and bow, cow, you will always reach the supreme way that abides.

1768.reading: If you seek the primal feet day and night, cow, you will see the fullness, the state of release that embraces.
1768.nuance: புல்லும் may be 'that embraces' (புல்லுதல்) or, less likely, 'grass', the cow's fodder; the first fits the sense and the second the herding frame. அல்லும் பகலும் makes the seeking constant.

1769.reading: Truth comes into the power of those who hold to the One alone, cow; in the state where you stand, know what is straight.
1769.nuance: ஒன்றைப் பிடித்தோர், those who have seized one thing, makes single-mindedness the condition of truth. The printed அரிவாயே would mean 'you will cut'; the sense wants அறிவாயே, 'you will know'.

1770.reading: Though you have everything, cow, if the Lord's grace is not there, reckon it as nothing and bow.
1770.nuance: இல்லாத் தன்மை, the nature of what is not, turns possessions into absence when grace is missing; the verse does not reject wealth, it makes grace its only value.

1771.reading: If you look closely, cow, without God's help there is nothing else; the father's holy feet are the life of life.
1771.nuance: ஆவிக்கும் ஆவி, the life of life, puts the Lord's feet inside the soul as its own animating breath; அத்தன் is father.

1772.reading: Is not he who is within Shakti more loving than a mother, cow? He will never leave those who love him.
1772.nuance: The mother image recurs at 1809. சத்திக்குள் ஆனவன் puts the Lord within his power, so the tenderness of the mother is Shakti's and the Lord is inside it.

1773.reading: Praise him, cow, who is the seed of release, who became the root substance, who is kin to Shakti.

1774.reading: If you bow with love at the Lord's holy feet, cow, you will see all your cruel deeds run away.
1774.nuance: The same claim as 1740, that worship of the feet, not knowledge or yoga, scatters karma; the verb விட்டோடும், they leave and run, makes the deeds flee like a frightened herd.

1775.reading: If you bow low at the feet of the moon-crested one, cow, Indra, Mal and the others will do your bidding.
1775.nuance: The reward is a Siddhar boast: the gods become servants of the devotee. Bowing low (தாழ்ந்து) is set against the gods' service, so humility before Siva is what makes one master of the rest.

1776.reading: Praising with the inner sense the twin feet of the Maker that the outer eye cannot see, cow, you will reach the height.
1776.nuance: கட்புலன் and உட்புலன், outer sense and inner sense, are paired again at 1801; worship is moved from the image the eye sees to a sense within.

1777.reading: If you cling close to that which became the void, which cannot be seen even when pointed at, cow, who will equal you?
1777.nuance: சூனியமானவத்தை is read as சூனியமான அத்தை, that which became the void. As at 1734, the void is the object to be clung to (ஒட்டிப் பிடி), not a denial; சுட்டியும் காண ஒண்ணா says it is past all pointing.

1778.reading: Those who do not reach the Lord by their own mind, cow, live in the world like hard trees.
1778.nuance: தானு is Sthanu, a name of Siva, 'the fixed one'; the irony is that those who fail to reach the fixed one become fixed themselves, like trees. தன் மனம் தன்னாலே stresses one's own mind as the means.

1779.reading: If you do not praise the light that is the good meaning called the word, cow, everything will tell you there is no state of release.
1779.nuance: சொல்லெனும் நற்பொருள் may be 'the good meaning that the word carries' or 'the good thing that is the Word itself', the Lord as utterance (1733). The last line is compressed: perhaps every thing declares release absent for such a person, perhaps every scripture says so.

1780.reading: Praise the great light held to be the pupil within the eye, the jewel of the sky, the light of the lamp.
1780.nuance: The section to many (பலரோடு கிளத்தல், 1780 to 1789) changes the address from the cow to everyone, in couplets ending போற்றீரே. The three images go from the body (the eye's pupil) to the cosmos (the sun, the sky's jewel) to the household lamp.

1781.reading: Worship and praise in the heart the sun that the fit faculties of mind, speech and body cannot reach.
1781.nuance: These are the three faculties (முப்பொறி) named in the invocation at 1732. The Lord is past all three, yet is served in the heart (நெஞ்சமதில்), which is not counted among them.

links.note: The same inner campaign: Kaduveli says take the fourfold fort within and cut and burn the forest called the thieving senses to see the house; Idaikkadar cuts the forest of ignorance with the sword of tapas and builds his own fort against death. Kaduveli captures a fort, Idaikkadar builds one.

Both keep the five senses from straying into their field: Tirumular turns back the five so they do not go into the millet field, and Idaikkadar drives the five goats out of the forest of taste, light, touch and sound and pens them in the space of yoga. Both master the senses by turning, not destroying them.

The two attachments Idaikkadar cuts are traditionally 'I' and 'mine', which the Kural says must be cut to enter a world above the gods'; Idaikkadar names what follows: the higher pleasure and union with the Supreme.

Both describe the seal at the palate by which the body's nectar is drunk: Tirumular raises the tongue to its shoot so the body's water rises like cane juice, and Idaikkadar closes the palate within and drinks the nectar. Idaikkadar adds that this is still subordinate to true knowledge.

Both climb the six centres to reach what lies above them: Tirumular counts the petals from the root and finds the feet of the Lord who has seen time at the end, and Idaikkadar seeks the gods of the six supports and then the Primal One above them.

Idaikkadar uses the mother twice for the Lord: here he is more loving than a mother and never leaves those who love, and at 1809 he guards every life as a mother does. The second extends the care from devotees to all lives.

Idaikkadar's two cowherds agree on the void: Thandavaraya Konar says Brahman must be known as சூனியம், and Narayana Konar tells the cow to cling to the one that became the void, past pointing. In both the void is the Lord to be held, not an absence.

Both call a human being who lacks the essential thing a tree: the Kural those without courtesy, however sharp, and Idaikkadar those who do not reach Siva by their own minds. Idaikkadar's tree also puns on தானு, Sthanu, the fixed one they fail to reach.

Both compare the Lord to the pupil of the eye: for Tirumular he is like the pupil to those who can see, and Idaikkadar praises the great light thought of as the jewel within the eye. In both the image places the Lord at the seeing centre, not among things seen.

source_issues: 1757 (idaikkadar:u2) is the refrain of 1758 to 1765 printed as its own unnumbered unit; the stanzas carry only the cue (தாந்).
1760: வீறு heads the list of sense objects where smell would be expected; possibly corrupt.
1765: the gloss on கோசம் (womb) does not fit கோசமைந்தும், which reads more naturally as the five sheaths.
